newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Up to 100,000 refugees flood Zairean town - U.N..
newsitem.headline: Up to 100,000 refugees flood Zairean town - U.N..

text.p: Tens of thousands of Rwandan refugees, possibly as many as 100,000, flooded into the eastern Zairean town of Ubundu over the weekend, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said on Monday.
WFP spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie said the sudden influx overwhelmed the four aid workers in Ubundu, 100 km (60 miles) southeast of the northeastern regional capital of Kisangani.
"Tens of thousands of refugees poured into Ubundu over the weekend and there are possibly as many as 100,000 there now," said Quintaglie, who added there were only hundreds in the town on Friday.

"The refugees are in very bad shape, they need food and medicine so we are trying today to kick our operation into the highest gear possible," she said. Sixty-five tonnes of food arrived in Ubundu on Thursday by rail from Kisangani.
"The refugees fled Tingi Tingi before it fell to the rebels and our reports indicate they are afraid, are talking about leaving Ubundu and feel threatened by the rebel advance," she added in Nairobi.
Tingi Tingi camp was abandoned by its 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees 10 days ago, shortly before it fell to the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo -Zaire.

Quintaglie said the WFP planned to send in more staff and four tonnes of high protein biscuits into Ubundu, its first airlift of food to the town, from Kisangani later on Monday but the plane was for the moment fogged in at Kisangani airport.
WFP was also sending 120 tonnes of food by rail from Kisangani to Ubundu but Quintaglie said the railway stopped on the west bank of the Zaire river and the refugees were on the eastern bank.
"There is only one boat to ship supplies across the river at the moment and local people say we might soon have to start moving water and medicine. It is a big problem," she added.

The Hutus, mostly refugees who fled Rwanda three years ago, live in fear of reprisals for the genocide of up to 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. They have been forced ever deeper into Zaire by a rebel offensive since October.
When they left Tingi Tingi camp, the refugees included Hutu former Rwandan soldiers and extremist militiamen, who had a leading role in the genocide and have fought alongside Zairean troops.
A U.N. mission to Tingi Tingi on Sunday found bedraggled and sick Rwandan refugees emerging from the jungle, saying they wanted to go home and thousands more were on the way.
Hundreds of refugees were found in the wreckage of Tingi Tingi camp. Most of them were malnourished and many were sick.

"More are coming in every day and they say there are thousands more coming from the forest. They say they want to go home," Martin Griffiths, U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region of central Africa, told Reuters at the camp.
"These we see here are in a very poor condition which is one of the determining factors in making them return to the camp."
It was the first time rebels have allowed aid agencies access to areas near the frontlines to the west. Tingi Tingi is 210 km (130 miles) southeast of Kisangani, which the rebels say is surrounded.
Griffiths said U.N. agencies might within a week be able to airlift out the weakest.

The U.N. refugee agency estimated on Sunday more than 700 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees had returned to the ruins of Tingi Tingi and 250 others have gone back to a makeshift camp at Amisi, which was seized by rebel forces a week or so earlier.

A U.N. refugee agency spokesman said any mass return of the refugees to Rwanda and Burundi depended on a ceasefire, which on Saturday was ruled out by rebel leader Laurent Kabila who wants ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko first to open talks with him.
